criterion_notes.c1: No. Although the introduction notes safe drinking water and wastewater disparities among Indigenous Peoples in Canada as motivating background, the review examines how Indigenous and Western knowledge systems and research methodologies are integrated across water research and environmental/resource management broadly (including sea ice, lakes/rivers, watersheds, marine conservation, and in 26% of records drinking water primarily focused on water quality and physical health), rather than examining household or community water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 reading: Under the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2, this study would pass Criterion 2 (plain=yes) because a subset of its 33-item extraction tool and thematic synthesis codes broad water governance, co-management, institutional arrangements, and whether reviewed articles acknowledged Aboriginal and treaty rights. Under the active narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, however, Criterion 2 is NOT met (narrow=no): the review's central phenomenon is epistemological and methodological knowledge co-production in research and environmental co-management, and it does not analyze any specific legal or administrative rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure rules, tariffs/cost recovery, discretion, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure governing access). Even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, the overall decision remains exclude because Criteria 1 and 4 are not met.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. The study is a systematic realist review of 279 screened records yielding 63 included peer-reviewed articles, theses/dissertations, and grey-literature reports, analyzed with a structured 33-question extraction tool.
criterion_notes.c4: No. Reported outcomes are bibliometric, methodological, and process findings about knowledge integration in research and management (e.g., authorship demographics, disciplines, CBPR methods, co-management recommendations, enhanced understanding of water governance, and generation of new knowledge), with no empirical outcomes reported on household or community water or sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or service exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: No. While the study design (systematic realist review), geographic setting (Canada), and unit of analysis (63 published documents) are clearly identifiable, an eligible service-access exposure and a water/sanitation service-access outcome are absent.

evidence_quotes.quote: As such, the purpose of this combined systematic and realist review (SRR) was to examine the extent, range, and nature of peer-reviewed and grey literature that discuss contemporary approaches to integrative Indigenous and Western knowledge systems in water research and management practices in Canada.

Our review confirmed that the research to date has predominantly focused on water in the context of drinking water (26%); those that did not, instead used water as an example of how Indigenous knowledge, ideas, and practices are applied to water and used in other environmental contexts

The research purposes for articles in this category linked water management strategies to the relationships between drinking water quality and physical health in an effort to improve both water and human health. These articles generally retained a focus on water quality

Articles that discussed water governance critically evaluated current governance regimes and governing bodies in order to determine methods that work and to identify the opportunity for alternative models.
In sum, 279 documents were reviewed, and 63 documents were included in our SRR.

Benefits that authors identified for taking an integrative approach were listed as enhanced understanding about a particular phenomenon, such as water governance (Cave, 2012; Finn, 2010; von der Porten, 2013). More often, however, these benefits were identified as new knowledge that translated (or could be translated) into cultural, and/or environmental (water), and/or human health benefits.

raw_response.exposure: Integration of Indigenous and Western knowledge systems and research methodologies in water research and resource management practices
raw_response.outcome: Bibliometric and methodological characteristics of reviewed literature, implementation of Indigenous knowledge in research or resource management plans, enhanced understanding of water governance, and new knowledge with potential cultural, environmental, or health benefits (no water or sanitation service-access outcomes reported)
raw_response.population_and_sample: 63 peer-reviewed articles, theses/dissertations, and grey-literature reports (from 279 screened records published 2000-2015) addressing integrative Indigenous (First Nations, Inuit, and Métis/Metis) and Western knowledge approaches to water research and management in Canada; unit of analysis is the published document
raw_response.rationale: Exclude under E01 (Wrong topic). This systematic realist review synthesizes 63 Canadian peer-reviewed and grey-literature documents on how Indigenous and Western knowledge systems and methodologies are integrated in water research and broad environmental/resource management (e.g., sea ice, watersheds, marine planning, and water quality/health research). Although drinking-water disparities are noted as background and broad water governance/co-management themes are catalogued (which would satisfy the plain wording of Criterion 2, though not the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope), the review does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access (c1=no), does not evaluate a rule-type legal/administrative mechanism governing service access (c2=no), and reports only bibliometric/epistemological research-practice findings rather than any service-access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcomes (c4=no).
raw_response.study_design: Systematic realist review of peer-reviewed and grey literature
